sentences.text: Validate the problem
Test whether a real, painful problem exists before you write code: a problem brief, honest interviews and a written decision.
Write the problem brief
State who has the problem, what they do about it today and why that is not good enough, on one page.
If you cannot write it plainly, you are not ready to interview anyone.
List the assumptions that would sink the idea
Separate what you know from what you hope.
Rank each assumption by how badly the idea fails if it is wrong, then test the top ones first.
Find people who have the problem
Recruit from the group your brief describes, not from friends.
Prefer people who dealt with the problem recently, because recent behavior is better evidence than opinion.
Interview about the past, not the future
Ask what happened the last time, what they tried and what it cost them.
Keep your solution out of the conversation.
Write notes the same day, in the same format every time.
Look for commitment, not compliments
Praise costs nothing.
Evidence is time, access, money or a written pilot commitment.
Record each person's response honestly, including a plain no.
Decide, and write the decision down
Set what you learned against your assumptions.
Choose to continue, change the problem or stop, and write the evidence behind the choice so someone else can read it.
A one-page problem brief
An ordered list of assumptions with a status for each
Interview notes in a single format
A written decision to continue, change or stop, with the evidence behind it
What good looks like
Validation is finished when a stranger could read your notes and reach the same conclusion you did.
That is a higher bar than "people liked the idea", and it is the bar that protects your time.
The problem brief names one kind of person, one situation and one thing they do about it today.
It does not name a market.
You have spoken with people who match the brief and do not know you, and every conversation is written down in the same format on the same day.
Some of those people have given you something that costs them, such as an introduction, access to their data, a second conversation or a written commitment to try a pilot.
You wrote down what would make you stop before the first interview, and you can say whether that line was crossed.
The decision to continue, change the problem or stop is in writing, with the evidence beside it.
Illustrative example, not a real company
A founder with years of experience in dental-practice administration wants to build scheduling software.
The first brief says that dental practices want better scheduling.
After a round of interviews with office managers, the notes say something narrower.
The pain is a canceled appointment that nobody fills in time, and two people described a spreadsheet they rebuild every Monday to track it.
The founder rewrites the brief around late-filled cancellations, drops the idea of a full scheduling system and asks both spreadsheet users for a second conversation.
Both agree.
The written decision reads: change the problem, then continue with the narrower one.
Decision aid: continue, change the problem or stop
Read the evidence you have against the rows below.
Pick the row that matches what you saw, not the one you hoped for.
What the interview evidence usually means and the next move
What the evidence shows
What it usually means
The next move
Several unconnected people describe the same problem in similar words, and each has already tried to fix it
The problem is real for this group.
Continue.
Write down who they are and move to design.
People agree the problem exists but have never tried to solve it
It may be a nuisance and not a priority.
Ask what would have to change for it to matter.
Change the problem or stop if nothing would.
Different people describe different problems
Your brief is too broad.
Narrow the group or the situation and interview again.
People like the idea but offer nothing: no time, no access, no commitment
Politeness, not demand.
Treat the idea as untested and ask for a small commitment in the next conversation.
The only enthusiastic people are friends or people who already know you
You have not yet reached the market.
Recruit people from your brief who do not know you before you decide.
People already pay in money or time to work around the problem
There is a budget, and the workaround is your real competitor.
Map what they use today and what it costs them.
Continue if you can describe a clear gap.
Common mistakes
Common mistakes when validating a problem
Mistake
Why it costs you
Do this instead
Interviewing friends and family
They want to be kind, so their answers say little about the market.
Recruit people who match your problem brief and do not know you.
Describing your solution while you ask
People react to the idea instead of describing their own situation.
Ask about the last time the problem happened.
Keep the idea out of the first conversation.
Counting compliments as demand
Praise is cheap and does not predict what a person will do.
Record what each person did, offered or committed to.
Stopping at the first enthusiastic yes
One keen person is a story, not a pattern.
Look for the same problem in similar words from several people who do not know each other.
Believing that nobody else does this
An empty field often means no one has a budget for the problem.
Map what customers use today, including spreadsheets and manual work, before you call the field empty.
Deciding the stopping rule after the results are in
You will bend the rule to fit the outcome you wanted.
Write the stop criteria before the first interview and check them at the end.
Evidence to check before you move on
Move to Design the product when each of these is true and you could show it to a stranger.
The problem brief reads clearly to someone outside your field in about two minutes.
Every assumption has a status: supported, contradicted or still untested.
Interview notes exist for every conversation, in one format, with the date.
The decision to continue, change or stop is written down with the evidence beside it.
A "stop" is a useful result.
It costs far less than building the wrong product, and your notes still show how you think.
Where WE can help
WE's Customer Relations and Market Development line covers customer discovery: interviews, notes and a summary of what buyers actually said.
It does not promise that conversations will turn into customers or revenue.
The service line page lists what it covers and what it does not.
Sources
The steps and the decision aid draw on the articles and templates below.
Each article names the public sources it read.
Customer discovery interviews without false positives
Write the problem brief before the code
Kill criteria: deciding in advance when to stop
Mapping the alternatives a customer already uses
Is your SaaS idea a business or a feature?
One-page problem brief
Customer interview guide
Design the product
Turn a validated problem into a version-one design: the shortest path to value, a written cut line and the decisions you will defer.
List the jobs the customer is hiring you to do
Write each job as a sentence from the customer's side, using the words they used in your interviews.
These sentences, not a feature wish list, are the brief for the design.
Map the shortest path to value
Draw the single route from first visit to the moment the customer gets what they came for.
Remove every step that is not on that route.
Sketch the key screens and test them on paper
Show low-detail sketches to people from your interviews and ask what they expect to happen next.
Fix the confusion now, while a fix costs a pencil line.
Draw the cut line
Sort every idea into three groups, which are must exist for the first customer to get value, can wait, and will not build.
Version one is everything above the line and nothing below it.
Choose well-understood components
Use proven parts for sign-in, billing and email unless one of them is your product.
Keep a short log of the choices you are deliberately deferring and the trigger that would reopen each.
Write acceptance criteria for what is above the line
For each item, write the observable result that means it is done.
A person who did not design it should be able to check it.
A list of customer jobs in the customer's own words
A path to first value, drawn from first visit to first result
Annotated screen sketches
A written cut line for version one
A log of deferred decisions
Acceptance criteria for every item above the line
What good looks like
A good design is specific enough that a team can build from it without guessing, and small enough that the first customer can reach the result in one sitting.
It does not have to be finished or beautiful.
Every item above the cut line traces back to a job a customer described in their own words.
The path to first value fits on one page, and there is no step on it that a customer would call optional.
The cut line is written down, and the items below it have a stated reason for waiting.
Each item above the line has an acceptance criterion that someone who did not design it could check.
Choices you are deferring sit in a log with the trigger that would reopen each one.
Illustrative example, not a real company
A founder building invoice reminders for small design studios has a long list of ideas: recurring invoices, a client portal, tax reports, a mobile app and reminder emails.
The job she heard in interviews was getting paid without an awkward conversation.
Her cut line keeps three items above it: create an invoice, send a reminder on a schedule, and see which invoices are overdue.
Everything else goes below the line with a note.
The acceptance criterion for reminders reads: a studio owner sets a schedule once and a reminder arrives on that date without further action.
A friend who has never seen the sketches can check it.
Decision aid: above the line or below it
Run each candidate feature through these questions in order.
The first question you answer no to decides where the feature goes.
Questions that place a feature above or below the cut line
Question
If the answer is yes
If the answer is no
Did a customer describe the job this feature does, in their own words?
Keep it on the list and ask the next question.
Below the line.
Write down which interview would change your mind.
Is the path to first value broken without it?
Above the line.
Ask the next question.
Can the job be done by hand for the first customers?
Do it by hand and watch what happens.
Can a proven component do the job, such as sign-in, billing or email?
Buy or adopt it, and place the choice in the deferred-decisions log.
Above the line, with an acceptance criterion.
Would you be embarrassed to release without it?
Check whether the embarrassment is about the customer or about you.
Only the first belongs above the line.
Common mistakes
Common mistakes when designing a first version
Mistake
Why it costs you
Do this instead
Designing for everyone
A product with no first customer in mind has no first path to value.
Name one kind of customer from your interviews and design for that person.
Copying a competitor feature list
You inherit years of someone else's decisions without their reasons.
Start from the jobs you heard in interviews and add only what a job needs.
Polishing visuals before the flow works
Beautiful screens hide a path that confuses people.
Test the flow with sketches first and add polish once the path holds.
Leaving the cut line unwritten
Scope grows quietly and the release date moves with it.
Write the line down and change it only through a recorded decision.
Building sign-in or billing from scratch
You spend weeks on parts that are not your product.
Use proven components and note what would make you revisit the choice.
Writing acceptance criteria as intentions
A line such as "easy to use" cannot be checked, so every review becomes an argument.
Write what a person can observe, in the customer's words.
Evidence to check before you move on
Move to Set up the company when you can show each of these.
The company setup comes before you build because the people who write code for you will be asked who owns it.
Every item above the cut line traces back to a customer job.
The path to first value fits on one page and has no step that a customer would call optional.
Someone outside your team has read the acceptance criteria and could tell whether a feature passes.
Deferred decisions are listed with the trigger that would bring each one back.
The design does not have to be finished or beautiful.
It has to be specific enough that a team can build from it without guessing.
Where WE can help
WE's Product and IT Development line covers architecture, an agile build in short cycles and a pilot environment where your first customers can use the product.
It does not run your live service or promise that a product will pass a particular audit.
The service line page lists the full scope.

Each article names the public sources it read.

Set up the company and its paperwork
Settle who owns what, bring the right questions to your own counsel and accountant, and keep signed records in one place before others write code for you.
Write down who is contributing what
For each founder, list the role, the time promised, any money put in and any work or code that existed before the company did.
Where a contribution is unclear, mark it as a question.
Turn the open points into questions for your counsel
Group the points into entity, equity and vesting, intellectual property, founder agreements, names and tax.
Write each as a question, so a meeting with counsel produces answers and not a general conversation.
Engage your own counsel and accountant directly
The company hires them, and they advise the company.
Share the questions in advance and ask each adviser what they need from you to give a firm answer.
Sign what counsel advises and keep the originals together
Keep every signed agreement, filing and receipt in one folder with an index.
Anyone who later does diligence on your company will ask for it, so build the habit now.
Ask your accountant which tax registrations apply
The company may need an employer identification number from the IRS and other registrations that depend on where you operate.
Ask your accountant what applies and apply through the official agency.
Keep a cap table that matches counsel's records
Record who holds what, when and under which agreement.
Reconcile your table with your counsel's records every time something changes, and note the date of the check.
A list of what each founder contributes
A list of questions for your counsel and accountant
A folder of signed agreements with an index
A short list of registrations and the status of each
A cap table that matches your counsel's records
This playbook does not give legal or tax advice, and it does not tell you which structure to choose.
It helps you arrive at your own counsel and accountant with clear questions and clean records.
They give the advice.
What good looks like
Good company setup is dull and well documented.
A stranger who reads your folder can tell who owns what, which agreements are signed and which questions are still open.
Each founder's contribution is written down, including anything that existed before the company did.
Every question you took to counsel has a written answer, or is marked open with a date.
Signed agreements sit in one folder with an index, and the copies are the signed ones.
Your cap table matches your counsel's records, and the date of the last check is on it.
You know which registrations the company needs, who is responsible for each and whether it is done.
Illustrative example, not a real company
Two friends plan a billing tool for veterinary clinics.
One has written most of the early prototype in evenings while employed elsewhere.
The other has the clinic contacts.
They have not written down who owns what.
Before they hire anyone to write code, they list their contributions, mark the prototype as an open question and note that one of them has an employment agreement to read.
They write a page of questions on entity, equity, vesting and ownership of the prototype, and send it to a lawyer they have hired.
The meeting is shorter, because the lawyer starts from their list.
Decision aid: questions to bring to your counsel
Use the table to build your list.
Each row names a topic, the question to ask and what to bring so the answer can be specific.
It does not say what the answer is.
Questions to bring to your own counsel when setting up the company
Topic
What to ask your counsel
What to bring
Entity
Which kind of entity fits our plans, and what does each choice change for us?
Your plan for the next two years, where the founders live and how you expect to be funded.
Founder equity
How should ownership be split and recorded, and what does vesting do in our case?
The contribution list and any understanding the founders already have.
Tax timing
Are there tax elections or deadlines connected to how our shares are issued?
Dates and terms for any shares or grants.
Ask your accountant as well as your counsel.
Ownership of work
Who owns the work created before the company existed, and what has to be signed?
A list of what was built, when and by whom, plus any employment or consulting agreements.
Open-source and third-party code
What do the licenses on the parts we use allow in a commercial product?
A list of the libraries and services you use.
Name
What should we check before we commit to a company or product name?
The names you are considering and where you plan to use them.
Customer documents
What terms and privacy documents do we need before customers sign up?
A description of what the product stores and who can see it.
The tax identifier

The IRS says that businesses, organizations and some retirement trusts need an employer identification number (EIN) to manage their taxes, and its list of reasons to get one includes hiring employees.
Whether and when your company needs one, and which other registrations apply, is a question for your accountant.
Ask early, since the answer affects what you do before your first hire.
Common mistakes
Common mistakes when setting up a company
Mistake
Why it costs you
Do this instead
Leaving the founder understanding unwritten
Memories differ when money or credit is at stake, and a later investor will ask what was agreed.
Write the understanding down and ask your counsel how to record it.
Using a generic template without asking
A template can answer a question you do not have and miss the one you do.
Bring your facts to your counsel and ask what has to change.
Writing code before ownership is settled
Work done before the company existed may belong to someone else.
Ask your counsel who owns existing work before anyone new writes code.
Treating an online article as legal advice
An article cannot know your facts, your state or your deadlines.
Use articles to prepare questions.
Take the answers from your counsel.
Keeping records across personal accounts
Nobody can find the signed copy when a buyer or investor asks.
Keep one company folder with an index and put every signed document in it.
Missing a dated deadline
Some filings and elections have dates that cannot be moved.
Ask your counsel and accountant for a list of dated deadlines and put them in a calendar.
Evidence to check before you move on
Move to Build and ship version one when you can show each of these.
The contribution list exists and has been read by every founder.
Your counsel has answered each question on your list, or the open ones carry a date.
Signed agreements are in one folder with an index.
Your cap table matches your counsel's records, with the check dated.
Where WE can help
WE's Professional-Services Coordination line helps your own counsel, accountant and other specialists get the context they need, and keeps a shared list of open questions with an owner for each.
WE is not a law firm or an accountancy, does not give legal or tax advice and does not engage specialists for you.
The service line page lists what it covers and what it does not.

Build and ship v1
Build the first release in short cycles, keep a release checklist, review against the cut line and put it in front of a small group.
Set a weekly rhythm
Choose one goal for the week, write it where the whole team can see it, and review it at the end.
A fixed rhythm makes slipping visible early, which is when it is cheapest to fix.
Build the riskiest path first
Build a thin working slice from the start of the path to the first result before you widen anything.
If the hardest part does not work, you learn it in week one rather than week ten.
Keep a release checklist from the first week
List what must be true before anyone outside the team uses the product, including data protection basics, accessibility, backups and a way to see errors.
Add to the list every time something surprises you.
Review against the cut line every week
Compare what was built with the written cut line.
When scope changes, write down what changed, why, and what moved below the line to make room.
Release to a small group you can talk to
Start with a few people you know by name, so you can watch what they do and ask what they expected.
Widen the group only when the first group can reach the result without help.
Write down what broke and what you learned
Keep a short release note and an ordered backlog that records the evidence behind each item.
The next cycle starts from that backlog, not from memory.
A working first release
A release checklist
Weekly review notes that show scope changes
A short release note
A backlog ordered by evidence
What good looks like
A good first release is small, working and watched.
The team can say what shipped this week, what moved below the cut line and why, and the people using it are people you can call.
Each week ends with a written review that compares what was built with the cut line.
A thin slice of the riskiest path worked early, so the hardest problem was found while it was still cheap.
The release checklist exists, carries dates and has been followed at least once, including the security and accessibility items.
A person outside your team reached the first result without you doing it for them.
You can undo a release.
The way back to the last good version was decided before the release, not during it.
Illustrative example, not a real company
A founder building a shift-swap tool for restaurants works with a small remote team across time zones.
Each Monday the team writes one goal for the week in a shared document, and each Friday the founder compares what was built with the cut line.
In the second week the review shows that a calendar export crept in.
The founder moves it below the line and writes why.
The first release goes to a few restaurant managers she has spoken with by name.
One of them cannot find the swap button, and the note from that session becomes the top backlog item.
Decision aid: ready to widen the release group
Before you move from a few named people to a wider group, answer each row.
A row you cannot answer yet is the next piece of work.
Checks before widening a first release
Check
Ready when
If not yet
The first result
A person outside the team reached it without help, and you watched.
Keep the group small.
Write down where they hesitated and fix that first.
Errors
You can see an error as it happens and say who it affected.
Add error reporting before more people arrive.
Way back
You know how to return to the last good version and have done it once.
Practice the rollback on a test copy before the next release.
Security baseline
The checklist items are done or have a dated reason for waiting.
Work through the baseline checklist and date each deferral.
Accessibility
A keyboard-only run through the path to first value works.
Fix the keyboard path before adding visual polish.
Customer data
You know what the product stores, where, and who can see it.
Write the list down.
Ask your counsel about anything you do not understand.
Backups
A restore has been tried, not only a backup taken.
Try a restore on a copy and write down what happened.
Standards to build against
A checklist is stronger when each line points to a public standard instead of a habit.
Two are worth putting on the first list.

The W3C's Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2 cover a wide range of recommendations for making web content more accessible, and the document is a W3C Recommendation dated 12 December 2024.
Put its success criteria on the release checklist in the first week, because fixing accessibility after launch touches everything that is already built.
NIST's Secure Software Development Framework, published as SP 800-218, describes a core set of high-level secure software development practices that can be integrated into each SDLC implementation.
Use it as a vocabulary for the security items on your checklist, and write down which practices you have adopted and which you have deferred.
Neither document tells you that your product is accessible or secure.
They give you a shared list to check against and to show to a reviewer.
Common mistakes
Common mistakes when building a first release
Mistake
Why it costs you
Do this instead
Adding scope without writing it down
The cut line stops meaning anything and the release keeps moving.
Record every change to scope with the item that moved below the line.
Leaving security and accessibility until later
Retrofitting them touches everything that is already built.
Put both on the release checklist in week one and build them in as you go.
Releasing to everyone at once
You cannot watch or talk to everyone, so you learn little.
Start with a small group you can reach by name.
Having no way to roll back
A bad release becomes an outage you cannot undo.
Decide how you will return to the last good version before you release.
Measuring activity instead of results
A busy team can still be building the wrong thing.
Review each week against the result the customer came for.
Keeping decisions in chat
A remote team loses them within days and re-argues them.
Write each decision in one shared place with its date and reason.
Evidence to check before you move on
Move to Hire your first team member when you can show each of these.
The release checklist exists, has dates on it and has been followed at least once.
Weekly review notes show what changed in scope and why.
The backlog is ordered, and each of the top items points to something you observed.
Version one will be incomplete.
That is expected.
What matters is that you can say exactly what is missing and what you saw that told you so.
Where WE can help
WE's Product and IT Development line builds in short cycles, shows working software at the end of each one and builds secure development practice in from the first repository.
It does not run your live service or offer round-the-clock support.
The service line page sets out what it covers and what it does not.

Hire your first team member
Define the outcome the role owns, settle the working relationship with your own counsel, interview with the same questions and prepare the first week.
Write the outcome the role owns
Describe what will be true when this person does the job well, in plain terms and without a list of tools.
If you cannot name the outcome, you are not ready to write the job description.
Settle the working relationship with your advisers
Decide with your counsel and accountant whether the person will be an employee, a contractor or something else.
Bring the facts about how the work will be directed and paid, because the answer depends on them.
Write a job description a candidate can answer
State the outcome, the first tasks, who the person works with and how you will judge the result.
Remove requirements that are habits of the last company you worked for.
Interview every candidate the same way
Use the same questions and the same scoring notes for everyone, and add a small piece of real work.
Decide before the interviews what a strong answer sounds like.
Put the offer in writing and have counsel review it
Write what the person is being offered, what the person is expected to do and what happens if either side ends the arrangement.
Have your counsel review the terms before you send them.
Prepare the first week before the first day
Arrange access to tools, one page that explains how the team works, a first piece of work with a clear result, and a person to ask.
Ask your counsel and accountant what paperwork the first day requires.
A one-page description of the outcome the role owns
A job description with first tasks and how the result will be judged
An interview scorecard
An offer reviewed by your counsel
A first-week plan
This playbook does not give employment, tax or immigration advice.
It helps you prepare the role and the facts, so your own counsel and accountant can tell you how to engage the person.
What good looks like
A good first hire starts with a clear outcome, a fair process and a written arrangement.
The new person can say in the first week what they are to deliver and how you will judge it.
The outcome the role owns is written down, and the founders agree on it.
Your counsel and accountant have been told the facts about how the work will be directed and paid, and you have their answer in writing.
Every candidate answered the same questions, and the scoring notes were written before the decision.
The offer is in writing, and counsel reviewed it before it was sent.
The first week has a plan with one piece of real work and a named person to ask.
Illustrative example, not a real company
A founder of a small inventory tool for bakeries has done all the support and the customer setup herself.
She writes one page that says the first hire will own customer setup, so that every new bakery reaches its first working report.
She tells her accountant and her lawyer how the work will be directed, whether the person will set their own hours and who will supply the equipment.
She asks both how to engage the person.
She interviews three candidates with the same four questions and a one-hour task based on a real setup.
The offer goes to her lawyer before it goes to the candidate.
Decision aid: what to settle before you choose how to engage someone
The right working relationship depends on facts.
Answer each row in writing and take the answers to your counsel and accountant.
They decide how to engage the person, not you and not an article.
Facts to settle and bring to your advisers before engaging a first team member
Question
Why it matters
Who to ask
Who will decide how, when and where the work is done?
The IRS asks whether the company controls, or has the right to control, what the worker does and how the job is done.
Your counsel and accountant.
Who pays for tools and equipment, and how is the person paid?
The IRS asks whether the business aspects of the worker's job are controlled by the payer.
Your accountant.
Is there a written agreement, and does the relationship have an ongoing character?
The IRS asks about written contracts, employee-type benefits and whether the relationship will continue.
Your counsel.
Where will the person live and work?
Engaging someone in another state or country can change the paperwork, tax and benefits.
Will the person own anything the company will rely on?
Work done for the company needs a signed agreement about who owns it.
Are you offering equity or a share in the outcome?
Equity has tax and legal consequences for both sides.
What will you do if it is not working?
A way to end the arrangement should be written before it is needed.
Facts to know before you ask
The IRS says that facts that provide evidence of the degree of control and independence fall into three categories, which it labels behavioral, financial and type of relationship.

Write down the value in the customer's terms

What good looks like
A good first sequence is small, personal and careful.
You can say why you wrote to each person, you can show what you sent and when, and nobody who asked you to stop received another message.

Illustrative example, not a real company
A founder of a tool that tracks warranty claims for appliance repair shops builds a list of twenty shop owners from the interviews she did earlier.
Beside each name she writes the reason, such as a comment about chasing manufacturers for payment.
Her message is four sentences and asks for a short call.
She asks her lawyer which rules apply and sets up the sender details and the opt-out before the first message goes.
Two owners reply, one asks to stop, and she records all three in the log.
In the next batch she changes only the opening line, so she can tell whether it made a difference.
What the FTC's compliance guide says
The Federal Trade Commission publishes a compliance guide for businesses on the CAN-SPAM Act.
Among its points, it says not to use false or misleading header information, and it says your message must include your valid physical postal address.
It also says to tell recipients how to opt out of receiving future marketing email from you, and that you must honor a recipient's opt-out request within 10 business days.
The guide is about email.
Rules for other channels, and rules in other countries, can differ.
Ask your counsel which apply to the messages you plan to send, and treat the guide as a list of questions, not a ruling on your case.

Build repeatable growth
Define your metrics in writing, run one channel long enough to learn, fix leaks before adding traffic and turn the results into a monthly review.
Define your metrics in writing
Write one definition each for monthly recurring revenue, churn, activation and the cost of winning a customer.

What good looks like
Repeatable growth means the result does not depend on one person having a good week.
The same steps, measured the same way, give you figures you can compare from one period to the next.

Questions to ask your counsel
These are questions to bring, not answers.
The answers depend on your company, your investors and where each of you is based.
Which instruments are open to a company like ours, and what does each one change for the founders?
Which rules apply when we look for investment, and what must we do before we speak with an investor?
What may we say about our company and our plans, and to whom?
Does each investor we want to approach need to meet any condition before we can talk with them?
What should we put in writing, and what should we hold back until an agreement is signed?
What will an investor ask to see about our contracts, our code and our agreements, and are our records ready?
What a public regulator says

The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) says that every offer and sale of securities must either be registered under the Securities Act of 1933 or rely on an available exemption from registration.
Whether and how that applies to your company is a question for your counsel.
Ask it before you speak with an investor, not after.
Common mistakes
Common mistakes when preparing for investors
Mistake
Why it costs you
Do this instead
Writing the pitch before ordering the evidence
Claims without records fall apart at the first question.
Order your records first and write the pitch from them.
Treating outside funding as the only route
You may give up more than you need to, or lose time on a route that does not fit.
Compare the routes in writing and choose by fit.
Speaking with investors before asking counsel
You may say or share things you cannot take back.
Bring your questions to your counsel and follow the advice before the first conversation.
Changing metric definitions between documents
An investor who sees two numbers for one measure stops trusting both.
Use one defined sheet for every document.
Contacting every investor you can find
Poor fit wastes your time and your name.
Choose a short list by stage and sector, with a reason for each.
Underestimating the founder time it takes
The company stalls while you are in meetings.
Write a time budget and protect time for customers.
Treating silence as a decision
You wait on someone who has moved on.
Record each contact in the log and decide what you will do next.

Founder playbooks
Step-by-step playbooks for building a SaaS company, from validating the problem to investor conversations, each with a decision aid and common mistakes.
Playbooks

The playbooks follow the order in which a SaaS company is usually built: validate the problem, design the product, set up the company, build and ship version one, hire the first team member, price the product, earn the first customers, run a first outbound sequence, build growth that repeats, and prepare for investor conversations.
They sit across three stages: Dream, Build and Grow.
Each playbook is a short sequence of steps.
Every step names the thing you should have in hand when it is done, so you can tell the difference between finishing a step and merely talking about it.

Each playbook also says what good looks like, offers a decision aid, lists the mistakes that cost founders the most time, gives an evidence check to run before you move on and ends with the sources it relied on.
You do not need to read them in order, but the later ones assume the earlier work exists.
If you cannot yet write down who has the problem and what they do about it today, start with the first playbook, not the last.
The playbooks are general working guides.
They are not a promise about how any company will perform, and they do not replace advice from your own lawyer, accountant or other qualified adviser.
The playbooks on company setup, hiring and investors say only what to ask your own counsel.
WE makes no promise of funding.
Each worked example is invented and labeled as an illustrative example, not a real company.
Step-by-step playbooks for building a SaaS company, in the order the work usually comes.
Each one gives the steps, what good looks like, a decision aid, the mistakes that cost founders the most time and the evidence to check before you move on.
